Porch
porch
n. (a covered entrance or colonnade before a building; rendering Hebrew ulam, Greek stoa and proaulion)
From the Latin porticus, a colonnade, from porta, a gate. Hebrew ulam is the vestibule standing before the temple proper — the threshold space a worshipper crossed before he was inside.

Biblical Definition

A porch is the space before the door, and Scripture gives it more weight than an entryway usually gets. Solomon's temple had one built to scale: “the porch before the temple of the house, twenty cubits was the length thereof, according to the breadth of the house” (1 Kings 6:3). The house of God did not open directly onto the street; there was a place to arrive before there was a place to enter, and the architecture taught approach. By the New Testament the temple's eastern colonnade was called Solomon's porch, and it became the ordinary place of public teaching and controversy: “Jesus walked in the temple in Solomon's porch” (John 10:23) — and within a few verses the Jews take up stones. After Pentecost the same colonnade is where the healed lame man held Peter and John and “all the people ran together unto them in the porch that is called Solomon's, greatly wondering” (Acts 3:11). The apostolic preaching happened in the same portico where Christ had been threatened. Its most poignant appearance is Peter's: “when he was gone out into the porch, another maid saw him” (Matthew 26:71). He had drawn back from the fire toward the exit, and the second denial met him there. A porch is a place of not-quite-in and not-quite-out, and the Gospel records what it costs to linger in one.

Webster 1828 Definition

The covered space before a door. The temple's porch taught approach, Solomon's colonnade held both Christ's teaching and the apostles' preaching — and Peter's second denial met him as he edged toward the exit.

PORCH, n. [L. porticus, from porta, a gate, passage or entrance.] In architecture, a kind of vestibule supported by columns at the entrance of temples, halls, churches or other buildings.

2. A portico; a covered walk.

3. By way of distinction, the Porch, a public portico in Athens, where Zeno taught his philosophy; whence his followers were called Stoics.

4. In Scripture, the vestibule before the temple; the porch of the house, 1 Kings 6.

5. Solomon's porch, a colonnade on the east of the temple, John 10.

Key Scripture

1 Kings 6:3 — "And the porch before the temple of the house, twenty cubits was the length thereof, according to the breadth of the house; and ten cubits was the breadth thereof before the house."

John 10:23 — "And Jesus walked in the temple in Solomon's porch."

Acts 3:11 — "And as the lame man which was healed held Peter and John, all the people ran together unto them in the porch that is called Solomon's, greatly wondering."

Matthew 26:71 — "And when he was gone out into the porch, another maid saw him, and said unto them that were there, This fellow was also with Jesus of Nazareth."

Modern Corruption

The porch becomes a settled address rather than a threshold — a place to be associated with Christ without entering — which is the position Peter occupied on the night he denied his Lord.

expand to see more

Matthew's account traces a drift with painful care. Peter follows afar off, sits with the servants to see the end, denies once by the fire, and then goes out into the porch, where the second denial finds him. Each step is a small withdrawal, and none of them is the decisive act; the decisive act is made possible by them. The porch is where a man is close enough to be recognised and far enough to deny, and it is a real spiritual location. Congregations are full of people standing in it — attached, familiar, unwilling to be identified. The remedy is not more atmosphere in the porch but a door, and Christ says plainly that whosoever shall confess him before men, him will he confess before his Father (Matthew 10:32).

The principle to recover is that God built the porch and meant it to be crossed. The temple vestibule was a place of preparation, not of residence, and the whole design moved inward — porch, holy place, holy of holies — toward a presence that could not be approached carelessly. That approach is now opened by a better way: the veil is rent, and believers have boldness to enter into the holiest by the blood of Jesus (Hebrews 10:19-20). It would be a strange thing to be given an opened holy of holies and to settle in the portico.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew ulam is the vestibule or porch before the temple. Greek stoa is a colonnade — the root of Stoic, from Zeno's teaching porch; proaulion is the forecourt of a house.

expand to see more

Hebrew ulam (H197) — a porch or vestibule; the space before the temple proper.

Hebrew misderon (H4528) — a colonnade or porch; the porch of Eglon's summer parlour.

Greek stoa (G4745) — a portico or colonnade; Solomon's porch in John 10 and Acts 3.

Greek proaulion (G4259) — a forecourt or porch; where Peter denied his Lord the second time.

Greek pulon (G4440) — a gateway or porch; the entry of a house or city.

Usage

"Of the temple's vestibule: the porch before the temple of the house (1 Kings 6:3)."

"Of the colonnade where Christ taught: Jesus walked in the temple in Solomon's porch (John 10:23)."

"Of Peter's second denial: when he was gone out into the porch, another maid saw him (Matthew 26:71)."
